Similarly, an experiment with strong alkali ($\text{NaOH}$) and weak alkali ($\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$) will prove that the bulb in the solution of $\text{NaOH}$ will give a brighter light and the bulb in the solution of $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ will give a dim light. So, it will be proved that $\text{NaOH}$ is a strong alkali and $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ is a weak alkali.

$\text{pH}$ is used as a unit to determine the nature of an aqueous solution, a measure of the acidity, alkalinity or neutrality of the solution. The $\text{pH}$ of a solution is the negative logarithm of concentration of hydrogen ions present in the solution. That means-

$$\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$$

Where $\text{p}$ is written in small hand letter and $\text{H}$ is capitalized.

$[\text{H}^+]$ expresses the molar concentration of $\text{H}^+$ ions; how many moles of $\text{H}^+$ ions are there in one liter solution.

The presence of $\text{H}^+$ in $1$ liter distilled water is $10^{-7}$ moles.

The $\text{pH}$ of distilled water $= -\log[\text{H}^+] = -\log(10^{-7})$

So, the $\text{pH}$ of distilled water $= 7$

When there is any ion within the third bracket in molarity unit, the concentration of the ion is expressed. If acid is added to distilled water and for this reason, the number of $\text{H}^+$ increases $10$ times to make it $10^{-6}$ moles per liter, the $\text{pH}$ of the solution will drop down.

$$\text{pH} = -\log[10^{-6}] = 6$$

The more the molarity of $\text{H}^+$ ion, the lesser the value of $\text{pH}$ will be.
